title.text: When to stop at a crossing

why_how.text: The handbook requires a stop between fifteen and fifty feet from the nearest rail whenever a signal, gate, flagger or train calls for it.
No driver or pedestrian may pass a crossing gate while it is closed or moving.

scenario.text: Sam approaches a crossing where the electric signal is flashing to warn of a train.

reasoning.text: A visible signal warning of a train requires a stop no more than fifty feet and no less than fifteen feet from the nearest rail.

result.text: Sam stops about thirty feet from the nearest rail, keeps as far right as possible, and waits until it is safe to cross.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the stopping zone at a crossing is measured in hundreds of feet.

correction.text: The fifteen hundred foot figure refers to an audible train, while the stopping zone itself is between fifteen and fifty feet from the rail.

prompt.text: Sam sees the crossing signal flashing for a train. How far from the nearest rail should Sam stop?

answer.text: No more than fifty feet and no less than fifteen feet.

rationale.text: A flashing signal triggers the stop, and the stopping zone is fifteen to fifty feet from the nearest rail.

narration.text: This chapter begins at railroad crossings, then moves on to city, rural and interstate driving and to vehicle lights. This first lesson covers the handbook's rules for when a stop at a crossing is required and where you must stop. You will review the stopping zone measured from the nearest rail, the signals, gates and flaggers that require the stop, the train situations that require it, the rule about crossing gates, how traffic lines up while stopped, and the penalty for breaking the railroad signal law. Two distances appear here, so keep track of which one is the stopping zone.

lines.text: No more than fifty feet from the rail.
Wait until you can cross safely.

narration.text: When the railroad statute's conditions apply, you must stop no more than fifty feet and no less than fifteen feet from the nearest rail, and wait until you can cross safely. So the stop has both a far limit and a near limit. Fifty feet is the farthest away you may stop, and fifteen feet is the closest you may stop. The stopping zone at a railroad crossing is between fifteen and fifty feet from the nearest rail, with closer than fifteen being too near and farther than fifty too far. The next slides cover the conditions that trigger this stop.

lines.text: A signal warns of a train.

narration.text: The stop is required when a visible electric or mechanical signal warns of an approaching train, or when a crossing gate is down, or when a flagger is signaling a train. These are the human-made warnings at a crossing. Any one of them is enough to require the stop. And no driver may go through, around or under a crossing gate or barrier while it is closed or moving, and pedestrians may not pass it in any way either. So when a gate is down or moving, the handbook's rule is simple: stop in the zone and do not pass the gate by any route.

lines.text: A train sounding within about fifteen hundred feet.
A train plainly visible and dangerously close.

narration.text: The train itself can also require the stop. The stop is required when a train within roughly fifteen hundred feet sounds a signal and is an immediate hazard, or when a train is plainly visible and dangerously close. So even at a crossing without working lights or gates, an approaching train that is sounding its signal nearby, or that is clearly visible and close, means you stop in the fifteen to fifty foot zone. These conditions sit alongside the signal, gate and flagger triggers. Any one of them is enough to require the stop.

lines.text: About fifteen hundred feet: the sounding train.
Fifteen to fifty feet: where you stop.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Two very different distances appear in this part of the handbook. The audible-train trigger refers to a train within roughly fifteen hundred feet, while the stopping zone itself is measured in tens of feet from the rail. Practice questions may ask where you must stop and offer fifteen hundred feet, or ask about the sounding train and offer fifty feet. Tie each number to its role. Roughly fifteen hundred feet describes how near a sounding train is. Fifteen to fifty feet describes where your car must stop, measured from the nearest rail.

lines.text: Keep as far right as possible.
One line unless four or more lanes.
Breaking the law is an infraction.

narration.text: While stopped for a crossing, keep as far right as possible and do not form two lines of traffic unless the road is marked for four or more lanes. Breaking the railroad signal law is an infraction, and an employer who knowingly lets a commercial driver break it also commits an infraction and faces a civil penalty. So the rules reach beyond the driver at the wheel. On an ordinary two-lane road, traffic forms one line on the right while waiting. And a company that knowingly allows its commercial drivers to break the signal law is also responsible under the law.

Here is a quick check: Sam approaches a railroad crossing where the electric signal is flashing to warn of an approaching train. How far from the nearest rail should Sam stop? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no more than fifty feet and no less than fifteen feet. A visible signal warning of a train is one of the conditions that requires the stop, and the stopping zone is between fifteen and fifty feet from the nearest rail. Sam keeps as far right as possible, waits until it is safe to cross, and never passes a closed or moving gate.

lines.text: Fifteen to fifty feet from the rail.
Never pass a closed or moving gate.

narration.text: Let us recap. When a stop is required, stop no more than fifty feet and no less than fifteen feet from the nearest rail, and wait until you can cross safely. The stop is required for a visible signal, a lowered gate, a signaling flagger, a train within roughly fifteen hundred feet that sounds a signal and is an immediate hazard, or a train plainly visible and dangerously close. No one may pass a closed or moving gate. Keep right in one line unless there are four or more lanes, and breaking the signal law is an infraction, for drivers and knowing employers.

why_how.text: The handbook says a train always has the right of way, even over emergency vehicles, and needs more than a mile to stop at fifty-five.
Each sign and control at a crossing calls for a specific response, from looking and listening to a full stop.

scenario.text: Pat reaches a rural crossing marked only by a crossbuck, with no lights or gates, and hears a train approaching.

reasoning.text: You must always yield to a train, even at a crossing marked only by a crossbuck with no lights or gates.

result.text: Pat yields and waits for the train to pass before crossing carefully.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a crossing with no lights or gates gives the car the right of way.

correction.text: At a crossbuck with no lights or gates you must still yield to any train, and at a crossbuck with flashing red lights you stop as for any flashing red signal.

prompt.text: Pat hears a train approaching a crossing marked only by a crossbuck. Who has the right of way?

rationale.text: You must always yield to a train, even at a plain crossbuck with no lights or gates.

narration.text: This lesson covers the signs and controls you find at railroad crossings and the response each one calls for. You will review the yellow and black advance warning sign, the train's right of way and stopping distance, how to approach a crossing, the crossbuck and the smaller sign beneath it, gates and signals, the rule that tracks are private property, and what flashing red lights at a crossbuck require. The handbook is clear that a train always has the right of way, and that idea runs through every rule in this lesson, whether the crossing has gates or only a sign.

title.text: The advance sign and the train

lines.text: Yellow and black RR sign: crossing ahead.
Trains always have the right of way.
More than a mile to stop at fifty-five.

narration.text: A yellow and black RR sign warns that a railroad crossing is ahead, so look both ways and listen, because you may need to stop. A train always has the right of way, even over police, fire and ambulance vehicles, and if the crossing has a stop sign, you must stop fully before crossing. A train going fifty-five miles per hour needs more than a mile to stop. So the advance sign is your first cue to slow, look and listen, and the train's right of way and long stopping distance are why the handbook asks you to be ready to stop every time.

At a crossing sign, approach carefully, be ready to stop for a train, move on carefully once it passes, and never stop on the tracks for any reason. The crossbuck is the X-shaped sign at the crossing itself, and a smaller sign beneath it shows when there is more than one track. Railroads are private property, so driving on or across tracks anywhere other than a designated crossing is illegal. So the advance sign tells you a crossing is ahead, the crossbuck marks the crossing, and the crossing is the only place where you may cross the tracks.

lines.text: Signals start: stop before the gates.
Moving through with gates down is unlawful.

narration.text: When crossing signals start, you must stop before the gates come down across your side, and moving through a crossing with the gates down is unlawful. This connects to the gate rule from the last lesson: no driver may go through, around or under a crossing gate while it is closed or moving. So the moment the signals begin, the handbook's direction for an approaching driver is to stop short of the gates. A later lesson covers the different rule for a driver who is already on the tracks when the signals start, so keep the approaching driver's rule separate.

lines.text: Flashing red lights: stop as for any flashing red.
No lights or gates: always yield.

narration.text: Some crossbucks have flashing red lights. Flashing red lights at a crossbuck mean you stop exactly as you would for any flashing red traffic signal. Other crossings have only the crossbuck, with no lights or gates. Even there, you must always yield to a train. So the controls at a crossing change what you do in detail, but never who has the right of way. With flashing lights, you stop. With only a crossbuck, you yield to any train. In every case, the train has the right of way, as the handbook states. With lights, stop; without them, yield.

title.text: Plain crossbuck, same right of way

lines.text: Lights: stop as for flashing red.
No lights: still yield to any train.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Practice questions sometimes suggest that a crossing with no lights or gates gives the car the right of way, because there is no signal telling you to stop. That is wrong. At a crossbuck with flashing red lights you stop as for any flashing red signal, while at a crossbuck with no lights or gates you must still yield to any train. A plain crossbuck does not change the train's right of way. So when a question describes an unmarked or lightly marked crossing, the answer still has the driver yielding to the train. Memory line: yield at every crossbuck.

lines.text: A crossbuck, no lights or gates.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Pat drives up to a rural railroad crossing marked only by a crossbuck, with no lights and no gates, and hears a train approaching. Who has the right of way? Work it out before reading on. The answer is the train, and Pat must yield. You must always yield to a train, even at a crossing marked only by a crossbuck with no lights or gates, and a train always has the right of way. Pat waits for the train to pass, then moves on carefully, never stopping on the tracks. The train always has the right of way, as the handbook states.

lines.text: Trains always have the right of way.

narration.text: To wrap up, a yellow and black RR sign warns that a crossing is ahead, so look both ways and listen. A train always has the right of way, even over emergency vehicles, and a train at fifty-five needs more than a mile to stop. Approach carefully, be ready to stop, and never stop on the tracks. The crossbuck marks the crossing, with a smaller sign for more than one track, and tracks may be crossed only at designated crossings. Stop before lowering gates, stop for flashing red lights, and yield to any train even at a plain crossbuck.

why_how.text: The handbook warns that a second train may follow the first, so you wait for the red lights to stop.
If the warning starts while you are on the tracks, the handbook says to keep moving, because the warning allows time to clear.

scenario.text: Kai is halfway across the tracks when the crossing lights begin flashing.

reasoning.text: If the lights start flashing or the gates begin lowering while you are on the tracks, keep moving and do not stop or back up.

result.text: Kai keeps driving across, through a gate that comes down beyond the car, since gates are flexible and cannot trap you.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a driver already on the tracks should stop or back up when the lights start flashing.

correction.text: Before the signals start you stop short of the lowering gates, but if you are already on the tracks you keep moving and do not stop or back up.

prompt.text: Kai is already on the tracks when the crossing lights start flashing. What should Kai do?

answer.text: Keep moving; do not stop or back up.

rationale.text: The warning allows time to clear, so a driver already on the tracks keeps going rather than stopping.

narration.text: This lesson covers what happens at the crossing itself: waiting after a train passes, the vehicles you should expect to stop in front of you, what to do if the warning starts while you are on the tracks, how crossing gates behave, and the danger of stopped traffic. The handbook draws a sharp line between a driver who is approaching the crossing and a driver who is already on the tracks. The two get opposite instructions when the signals start. Keeping that difference clear is the main goal of this lesson, and practice questions test it often.

lines.text: Do not start the moment it passes.
A second train may come either way.
Wait for the red lights to stop.

narration.text: Do not start moving the moment a train passes, because a second train may be coming either way. Wait until the red lights stop flashing. Also expect to stop behind vehicles that must stop at crossings, such as school buses, passenger carriers, for-hire vehicles and placarded vehicles hauling explosives or hazardous materials. So at a crossing, two kinds of waiting are common. You wait after a train for the lights to stop, and you wait behind buses and placarded vehicles that make required stops at the crossing even when no train is in sight.

lines.text: Do not stop or back up.
The warning allows time to clear.

narration.text: If the lights start flashing or the gates begin lowering while you are on the tracks, keep moving. Do not stop or back up, since the warning allows time to clear. Crossing gates are flexible and cannot trap you, so drive through a gate that comes down beyond you. Stopping to back up could stall the car. So for a driver already on the tracks, the handbook's instruction is to continue across, even if a gate lowers ahead. The gate is built to give way, and stopping or reversing on the tracks is the outcome the handbook warns against.

Gates will not trap you, but stopped traffic can. So make sure the traffic ahead will not halt and leave you on the tracks. This is a check you make before you start across. If the cars ahead are backed up toward the crossing, wait on your side until there is room for your whole car beyond the tracks. Never stop on the tracks for any reason, as the earlier lesson stated. Gates are flexible, but a line of stopped cars ahead is not, and it could leave your car sitting on the tracks with nowhere to go. Never stop on the tracks.

lines.text: Already on the tracks: keep moving.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The handbook gives opposite instructions depending on where you are when the signals start. Before the signals start you stop short of the lowering gates, but if you are already on the tracks when they start you keep moving and do not stop or back up. Practice questions often describe a driver on the tracks and offer stopping or backing up as the safe choice. It is not. Find the car's position first. Short of the tracks means stop before the gates. On the tracks means keep driving across, even through a gate that lowers beyond you.

Here is a quick check: Kai is halfway across the railroad tracks when the crossing lights begin flashing and the gates start to lower. What should Kai do? Work it out before reading on. Kai should keep moving and not stop or back up. If the lights start flashing or the gates begin lowering while you are on the tracks, the warning allows time to clear. If a gate comes down beyond the car, Kai drives through it, because crossing gates are flexible and cannot trap you, while stopping to back up could stall the car. Gates cannot trap you.

lines.text: Wait for the lights after a train.

narration.text: Let us recap. Do not start moving the moment a train passes, because a second train may be coming either way; wait for the red lights to stop. Expect to stop behind school buses, passenger carriers, for-hire vehicles and placarded hazardous material vehicles. If the lights start or gates lower while you are on the tracks, keep moving and do not stop or back up, and drive through a gate that comes down beyond you. Gates will not trap you, but stopped traffic can, so make sure the traffic ahead will not leave you on the tracks.

why_how.text: Every North Carolina crossing posts a Blue Sign with the information needed to reach the railroad in an emergency.
If a vehicle stalls on the tracks, the handbook puts getting out and away first.

scenario.text: Riley's car stalls on the tracks at a quiet crossing.

reasoning.text: Get out right away and walk quickly along the road to a safe spot away from the tracks, and only then call the railroad using the Blue Sign.

result.text: Riley leaves the car, walks away from the tracks, then calls the number on the Blue Sign.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you should call the railroad from inside a stalled car before getting out.

correction.text: A stalled car on the tracks means get out and move away first, and only then call the railroad using the Blue Sign.

prompt.text: Riley's car stalls on the tracks. Should Riley call the railroad first or get out first?

answer.text: Get out and move away first, then call.

rationale.text: The handbook's order is leaving the tracks first, then using the Blue Sign to call the railroad.

lines.text: A car stalled on the tracks.

narration.text: This lesson covers emergencies at railroad crossings. You will review the Emergency Notification System Blue Sign that every North Carolina highway-rail crossing must post, what information it shows, why calling the railroad through it matters, and what to do if your vehicle stalls on or near the tracks. The handbook sets a clear order for a stall: first get yourself to safety, then call. You will also see who to contact for a crossing emergency compared with who to contact about a damaged or missing sign. The order of steps is what practice questions test most.

lines.text: Posted at every crossing, each direction.
Crossing ID, railroad name, emergency phone.
Each crossing has a unique number.

narration.text: Every highway-rail crossing in North Carolina must post an Emergency Notification System Blue Sign in each direction, showing the crossing ID number, the railroad name and an emergency phone number. Using the Blue Sign to call the railroad directly is the fastest way to get a train stopped in an emergency, and each crossing has its own unique USDOT identification number. So the Blue Sign gives you everything the railroad needs: which crossing you are at, which railroad runs it, and a number to call. Calling that number is the handbook's fastest route to stopping a train.

lines.text: Walk along the road to a safe spot.

narration.text: If your vehicle stalls on or near the tracks, get out right away and walk quickly along the road to a safe spot away from the tracks. The instruction is immediate: you leave the vehicle first. The Blue Sign number reaches the railroad for crossing emergencies, while damaged or missing signs go to the Federal Railroad Administration. So there are two different contacts. A stalled car or other emergency at a crossing goes to the railroad through the Blue Sign. A damaged or missing sign is reported to the federal agency instead. Keep the two contacts separate.

lines.text: Get out and away from the tracks.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some learners assume the first step after a stall is to call for help, perhaps from inside the car. The handbook sets the order the other way around. A stalled car on the tracks means get out and move away first, and only then call the railroad using the Blue Sign, not the other way round. On practice questions, an option that calls first, or that stays in the vehicle to keep trying the engine, does not match the handbook. The memory line is short: leave first, then call. Safety comes before the phone call.

lines.text: Riley's car stalls on the tracks.
Call first or get out first?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Riley's car stalls on the tracks at a quiet crossing, and no train is in sight yet. Should Riley call the railroad first, or get out first? Work it out before reading on. Riley should get out right away and walk quickly along the road to a safe spot away from the tracks, and only then call the railroad using the number on the Blue Sign. The Blue Sign shows the crossing ID number, the railroad name and the emergency phone number, and calling the railroad directly is the fastest way to get a train stopped.

lines.text: Damaged signs go to the federal agency.

narration.text: To finish, every North Carolina highway-rail crossing posts a Blue Sign in each direction with the crossing ID number, railroad name and an emergency phone number, and each crossing has a unique identification number. Calling the railroad through the Blue Sign is the fastest way to get a train stopped. If your vehicle stalls on or near the tracks, get out right away and walk to a safe spot away from the tracks, and only then call. The Blue Sign number is for crossing emergencies, while damaged or missing signs are reported to the Federal Railroad Administration.

why_how.text: In the city, the handbook focuses on bicyclists, wrong lanes, blind spots and lane use on one-way streets.
The handbook says rural and secondary roads can be more dangerous than heavy city traffic.

scenario.text: Morgan realizes at the last moment that the car is in the wrong lane for a left turn downtown.

reasoning.text: If you find you are in the wrong lane for a turn in the city, continue to the next intersection and turn there.

result.text: Morgan goes straight and turns at the next intersection instead.

claim.text: Many people think rural roads are always safer than heavy city traffic.

correction.text: Rural roads are often more dangerous than heavy city traffic because they may be narrower, darker and faster.

prompt.text: Morgan is in the wrong lane for a turn downtown. What should Morgan do?

answer.text: Continue to the next intersection and turn there.

rationale.text: The handbook's fix for a wrong-lane turn in the city is to go on to the next intersection.

narration.text: This lesson covers driving habits for city streets and for rural roads. In the city, you will review the risk to bicyclists when you turn right, what to do in the wrong lane for a turn, how to tell when you are riding in another driver's blind spot, and how lanes are used on one-way streets. Then you will look at rural roads, which the handbook says are often more dangerous than heavy city traffic, and at secondary roads, which have their own hazards. Each habit comes straight from the handbook, with the reasons the handbook gives for it.

lines.text: Cyclists ride to the right of cars.
Right turns put straight cyclists at risk.
Wrong lane? Turn at the next intersection.

narration.text: Because bicyclists ride to the right of cars, a cyclist going straight through an intersection is at risk from a motorist turning right. So before a right turn, check for a cyclist on your right who may be continuing straight. If you find you are in the wrong lane for a turn in the city, continue to the next intersection and turn there. The handbook does not ask you to force the turn from the wrong lane. Going on to the next intersection keeps your path predictable for the drivers and cyclists around you, and costs only a short detour.

lines.text: No inside mirror in view: likely a blind spot.

narration.text: Avoid riding alongside another car. When the forward car's inside mirror is out of your view, you are likely sitting in its driver's blind spot. Do not weave between lanes. On a one-way street, use the center lanes for through travel and the outside lanes for turns. So the handbook's city habits are about staying visible and predictable. Do not linger beside another car where its driver cannot see you, and do not dart from lane to lane. On one-way streets, choose your lane by where you are going: center for straight ahead, outside for a turn.

lines.text: Secondary roads: steep hills, sharp curves.

narration.text: Rural roads are often more dangerous than heavy city traffic, because they may be narrower, darker and faster. Secondary roads tend to have steeper hills, sharper curves and short sight distances, so they cannot be driven safely at speeds suited to primary highways. So the handbook reverses a common assumption. Light traffic does not make a road safe. On a narrow, dark rural road, or a secondary road with steep hills and sharp curves, the safe speed is lower than on a primary highway, because you cannot see as far ahead or react as easily.

lines.text: Rural roads can be more dangerous.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many learners assume that a quiet country road is safer than busy city streets. The handbook says otherwise. Rural roads are often more dangerous than heavy city traffic because they may be narrower, darker and faster, and secondary roads tend to have steeper hills, sharper curves and short sight distances. On practice questions, an option claiming that rural roads are always safer, or that secondary roads can be driven at primary highway speeds, does not match the handbook. The memory line is simple: narrow, dark and fast.

lines.text: Wrong lane for a downtown turn.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Morgan is driving downtown and realizes at the last moment that the car is in the wrong lane for the left turn Morgan planned to make. What should Morgan do? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to continue to the next intersection and turn there. If you find you are in the wrong lane for a turn in the city, the handbook says to go on to the next intersection rather than turn from the wrong lane. Morgan also avoids weaving between lanes, and stays out of other drivers' blind spots along the way.

lines.text: Wrong lane: turn at the next one.

narration.text: Let us recap. Because bicyclists ride to the right of cars, a cyclist going straight is at risk from a motorist turning right. In the wrong lane for a city turn, continue to the next intersection and turn there. Avoid riding alongside another car; if you cannot see its inside mirror, you are likely in its blind spot. Do not weave, and on one-way streets use the center lanes for through travel and the outside lanes for turns. Rural roads can be narrower, darker and faster, and secondary roads cannot be driven safely at primary highway speeds.

why_how.text: The handbook says interstates are safer because opposing traffic is separated and there are fewer entry points and no crossings, sharp curves or signals.
Entering, exiting and handling mistakes each follow set steps on the interstate.

scenario.text: Taylor misses the planned exit on an interstate.

reasoning.text: If you miss your exit, do not slow down, back up or turn around; go on to the next exit and find a way back from there.

result.text: Taylor continues to the next exit, leaves the interstate there, and finds a way back.

claim.text: Common mistake: treating a missed exit and a wrong-way entry the same way.

correction.text: A missed exit is handled by driving on to the next one, while a wrong-way entry is handled by pulling onto the right shoulder, stopping and turning around when clear.

prompt.text: Taylor misses the planned exit on the interstate. Should Taylor back up on the shoulder?

answer.text: No. Taylor should go on to the next exit and find a way back from there.

rationale.text: A missed exit is never fixed by slowing, backing up or turning around; the handbook says to use the next exit.

narration.text: This lesson covers interstate driving from start to finish. You will review why the handbook calls interstates safer, how to enter using the acceleration lane, which lanes to use and how to avoid tailgating, rest stops and breakdowns, how to exit using the deceleration lane, why crawling below the limit is dangerous, and what to do after two common mistakes: missing your exit and entering the wrong way. The handbook gives specific steps for each, and practice questions often place two of them side by side, so pay attention to how they differ.

lines.text: No crossings, sharp curves, stops or signals.

narration.text: Interstates are safer because opposing traffic is separated, entry and exit points are fewer, and there are no railroad crossings, sharp curves, stop signs or traffic signals. When entering an interstate, stay in the acceleration lane until you match the speed of traffic, then merge safely. So the acceleration lane is where you bring your speed up to the speed of the traffic you are joining. Once you are moving at that speed, you merge into a safe gap. Merging before you match the speed of traffic is not what the handbook describes.

lines.text: Keep right; pass on the left.
Do not drive far below the limit.

narration.text: On the interstate, keep right and use the left lanes to pass. Avoid tailgating by using the two-second rule, since rear-end crashes are among the most frequent there. It is also dangerous to drive far below the posted limit on the interstate, so follow the flow of traffic as long as you are not speeding. So the handbook's interstate habits are to stay right except to pass, keep at least two seconds behind the vehicle ahead, and move with the flow of traffic within the speed limit rather than far below it. Keep right except to pass.

lines.text: Rest at least every hundred miles.
Never stop in a travel lane.
Breakdown: off the road, white cloth, hood up.

narration.text: Stop at rest areas often, ideally at least once every one hundred miles, and never stop in a travel lane. After a breakdown, get well off the road, tie a white cloth to the antenna or the left door handle, and raise the hood. At night, turn on the emergency flashers or parking lights. So a planned stop belongs at a rest area, and an unplanned stop after a breakdown belongs well off the road with clear signals that you need help. In neither case does the handbook allow stopping in a travel lane. Never stop in a travel lane, as the handbook says.

lines.text: Move into the deceleration lane first.
Then keep to the exit speed.

narration.text: To exit, signal well ahead, move into the deceleration lane without slowing first, and then keep to the posted exit speed. On entry you speed up in the acceleration lane to match traffic, while on exit you move into the deceleration lane before slowing down. So the two ramp lanes mirror each other. Entering, you use the lane to build speed before joining traffic. Exiting, you leave the travel lanes first and then slow down in the deceleration lane. Slowing in a travel lane before reaching the exit lane is the step the handbook leaves out.

lines.text: Missed exit: go to the next one.
Never slow, back up or turn around.
Wrong way: right shoulder, stop, turn when clear.

narration.text: If you miss your exit, do not slow down, back up or turn around. Go on to the next exit and find a way back from there. If you enter an interstate going the wrong way, pull onto the right shoulder and stop, then turn around when the way is clear. Watch for DO NOT ENTER signs to avoid this. So the two mistakes get different fixes. A missed exit is solved by continuing forward. A wrong-way entry is solved by getting onto the right shoulder, stopping, and turning around only when the way is clear. Watch for DO NOT ENTER signs.

Here is a quick check: Taylor misses the planned exit on an interstate and is tempted to back up along the shoulder to reach the ramp. Should Taylor do that? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. If you miss your exit, do not slow down, back up or turn around; go on to the next exit and find a way back from there. Backing up and turning around are reserved for a different situation in the handbook: after a wrong-way entry, you pull onto the right shoulder, stop, and turn around when the way is clear. Take the next exit.

lines.text: Missed exit: take the next one.

narration.text: To wrap up, interstates are safer because opposing traffic is separated, entry points are fewer, and there are no crossings, sharp curves, stop signs or signals. Match the speed of traffic in the acceleration lane, keep right, pass on the left and use the two-second rule, and do not drive far below the limit. Rest at least every hundred miles and never stop in a travel lane; after a breakdown, get well off with a white cloth and the hood up. Exit through the deceleration lane before slowing. After a missed exit, take the next one; after a wrong-way entry, use the right shoulder.

why_how.text: The handbook sets how far high and low beams should let you see a person at night.
Taillights and the plate light have their own visibility distances, and badly aimed headlights cause glare.

scenario.text: Lee drives at night on a dark rural road with the low beams on.

reasoning.text: At night you should be able to see a person two hundred feet away with high beams and seventy-five feet away with low beams.

result.text: With low beams on, Lee expects to see a person at about seventy-five feet, compared with two hundred feet on high beams.

claim.text: Common mistake: mixing up the high beam and low beam distances.

correction.text: High beams should reveal a person at two hundred feet and low beams at seventy-five feet.

prompt.text: Lee has the low beams on at night. How far away should Lee be able to see a person?

rationale.text: Low beams should reveal a person at seventy-five feet, compared with two hundred feet for high beams.

title.text: Lights that see and are seen

narration.text: This final lesson in the chapter covers vehicle lights. Some lights help you see, and others help you be seen. You will review how far high beams and low beams should let you see a person at night, what can knock headlights out of aim and cause glare, and how far taillights and the license plate light must be visible. There are four distances in this lesson, each tied to a specific light, so practice questions often swap them. As you go, link each number to its light rather than memorizing the four figures as a bare list.

lines.text: High beams: a person at two hundred feet.

narration.text: At night you should be able to see a person two hundred feet away with high beams and seventy-five feet away with low beams. Headlights also have to be aimed correctly. Badly aimed headlights glare into the eyes of other road users. Vibration can knock them out of line, and a heavily loaded rear can tilt the beams up. So the handbook ties headlights to two concerns: how far they let you see, and whether they are pointing where they should. A heavy load in the trunk or ordinary vibration can change the aim enough to cause glare.

lines.text: Taillights: red, visible at five hundred feet.
Plate light: white, readable at fifty feet.

narration.text: Taillights must be red and visible from at least five hundred feet. A white light must make the license plate readable from at least fifty feet. So the rear lights have their own distances, separate from the headlight distances. The taillights are about being seen from far behind, at five hundred feet. The plate light is about making the numbers on the plate readable from fifty feet. Together with the headlight figures of two hundred feet and seventy-five feet, these make four distances, each belonging to a different light on the vehicle.

Here is the trap. High beams should reveal a person at two hundred feet and low beams at seventy-five feet, while taillights must be visible at five hundred feet and the plate light must light the numbers at fifty feet. Practice questions may give the taillight figure for high beams, or swap the high and low beam numbers. Match each number to its light. Two hundred goes with high beams, seventy-five with low beams, five hundred with taillights, and fifty with the plate light. The memory line for the headlights is short: high far, low near.

Here is a quick check: Lee is driving at night on a dark rural road with the low beams on. How far away should Lee be able to see a person? Work it out before reading on. The answer is seventy-five feet. At night you should be able to see a person two hundred feet away with high beams and seventy-five feet away with low beams. The other two distances in this lesson belong to rear lights: taillights must be visible from at least five hundred feet, and the plate light must make the plate readable from at least fifty feet.

To finish the chapter, at night you should be able to see a person two hundred feet away with high beams and seventy-five feet away with low beams. Badly aimed headlights glare into the eyes of other road users, and vibration or a heavily loaded rear can throw them out of aim. Taillights must be red and visible from at least five hundred feet, and a white light must make the license plate readable from at least fifty feet. Keep the four distances tied to their four lights, and you will be ready for questions that try to swap them.
